maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext:
The two railway companies should have had the hon. member for Fraser Valley in their employ. I made the statement then that we were able to buy good Canadian wheat and bring it from Japan at a lower cost than it could be brought from the prairie provinces. The railways could not overcome that argument because I had the shipping bills to prove my case. I was able to prove every point of my case, yet the hon. member ridicules a statement I made which the railway lawyers could not or did not care to dispute very seriously. I do not intend to use up all my time in refuting the hon. member for Fraser Valley because he stands refuted without any further statements from me.
I should like to deal now with some of the remarks made the other evening by the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Vien), whom I was rather surprised to see entering
the debate to oppose this bill. The hon. member is a former member of the board of railway commissioners, and I should like to deal with some of the remarks he made in connection with the bill. He stated that the rate was an export rate and that it was intended to help Canadian producers. What about the domestic producers? What about the producers of butter, cream, poultry and eggs in British Columbia? Are they not to be helped? I contend that it would be far better to help the domestic producer of bacon, eggs, poultry and other agricultural products rather than to ship our grain, including barley, to Europe and elsewhere and then have to meet in hams and bacon on the old country and other markets the competition of people who are able to procure good Canadian grain at fifty per cent less than the domestic producer has to pay. If export markets have been restricted during the last few years it is strange that no change has taken place in our policy in an endeavour to encourage domestic markets. Producers of poultry, eggs, butter, hams, bacon and so on should be given a better chance to compete, and with some degree of fairness and equity, against foreign competitors.
Then the hon. member 6aid that we must distinguish between a paying and a losing rate. As I have previously stated, the railways have no expert capable of giving the cost of hauling grain. I challenge the hon. member for Outremont, as I did the lawyers before the board, to deny that the export rate to British Columbia is a paying one. If the railway companies can haul seventy or eighty million bushels of wheat at a paying rate, why then should the people of British Columbia be called upon to pay twice that rate? I asked them to produce figures to disprove my statement that it was a paying rate, but for some reason or another they did not do so. I then reversed the argument. I said:	Assuming for a moment, which I do
not, that it is a losing rate, is it fair that the people of British Columbia should be called upon to pay the deficit so that their foreign competitors may obtain grain at fifty per cent of the cost which we in British Columbia have to pay? I submit that it is most unfair. The statement was made before the board that they were accused of flattening out the Rockies. Well, a large proportion of our people to-day are still under the impression that when going into British Columbia you have to go up one side of a mountain and down the other, but I would point out that as a matter of fact we have in our province the finest railway grade in

Railway Act

Rates on Grain
the whole of Canada. The grade is one-half of one per cent over the Canadian National, and that railway can take sixty cars either into British Columbia or from that province into the prairies, whereas its competitor, the Canadian Pacific railway, is faced with an averaged grade of 2-2 per cent, a very heavy grade indeed, so that it can take only twenty-five cars as its limit.
If I might offer one suggestion in connection with a reorganization of the railways it would be this. If we are looking for economy and efficiency, I submit that in carrying freight, to the Pacific coast at least, the Minister of Railways should urge that it be carried by the railway that can carry it, and that is the Canadian National. As I say, they have a grade of one-half of one per cent and can take into Vancouver or New Westminster three times as many cars as the Canadian Pacific railway can. As a matter of fact, they could take more, but owing to an arrangement with labour or the conductors they have agreed to take no more than sixty at one time.
Can hon. members visualize what happens with grain going into British Columbia, a whole trainload of say sixty cars, with one engine and one crew? Maybe forty or fifty cars in that trainload are carrying freight	at	20| cents per hundred	pounds,while the back portion of the train, consisting of cars of goods for consumption in British Columbia is charged 411 cents. Is there any equity	or	justice in that?	There	is notWe have a case that cannot be successfully disputed, and in the few minutes that remain to me	I	will indicate the	reasons	why Ihope and	believe that the	present	Liberal
administration will do far more than the last government did; for invariably their argument has been that the House of Commons is not the place to fight freight rates. They have contended that we should go before the board of railway commissioners. I am now going to read order in council, P.C No. 886, of June 5, 1925, issued by the last Liberal administration under the leadership of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), giving directions to the board of railway commissioners to equalize freight rates. I think hon. members will agree with me, when I read this order in council, that its language is as plain as any could possibly be to the layman. But we all know what lawyers are and how they can twist words. That is no reflection on you, Mr. Speaker.
It will be remembered that in 1925 the Liberal administration of the day dealt with this matter in the House of Commons; it was not the board of railway commissioners

that dealt with it. It is true that administration omitted to put into the amendment to the Railway Act the same provision with respect to grain going west as was made in connection with grain going east to Fort William; but having regard to that error, this is the direction the government of that day gave to the board, and I make the positive assertion that the board disobeyed the order of parliament. This is the order, and I would ask laymen at least among hon. members to pay particular attention to it; I should be afraid to ask lawyers to construe it, for I have had some experience with them:
The committee are of the opinion that the policy of equalization of freight rates should be recognized to the fullest possible extent as being the only means of dealing equitably with all parts of Canada and as being the method best calculated to facilitate the interchange of commodities between tlie various portions of the dominion, as well as the encouragement of industry and agriculture and the development of export trade.
I will not read the whole of it; I will come to what I consider the meat of this order, so far as the adjustment of freight rates is concerned:
The committee are further of the opinion that as the production and export of grain "and flour forms one of the chief assets of the dominion, and in order to encourage the further development of the great grain growing provinces of the west, on which development the future of Canada in large measure depends, it is desirable that the maximum cost of the transportation of these products should be determined and known, and therefore are of opinion that the maximum established for rates on grain and flonr, as at present in force under the Crowsnest pass agreement, should not be exceeded.
Now there is omission No. 1; the board did not obey that order, and they do not yet know what it costs to haul grain. Then further down:
The committee therefore advise that the board be directed to make a thorough investigation of the rate structure of railways and railway companies subject to the jurisdiction of parliament, with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rate structure, which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities.
I do not know what plainer language could be written into an order than that-equal to all persons and localities, and as I have pointed out, over the Canadian National road into British Columbia we have the lowest grade on any portion of the railway system in Canada. That cannot be too often repeated. But even if it did cost the Canadian Pacific a little more, which I doubt, to build a railway into British Columbia-and

Railway Act-Rates on Grain
I know that they have in some parts a grade of 2;2-let me tell lion, members what that railway has received in return. It got a cash subsidy of 125,000,000; constructed railway including service, $38,000,000; cash in exchange for subsidy lands, $10,000,000, and 18,206,985 acres of selected lands -valued at the time of earning at $27,310,000, making a total value of subsidies from the people of this country of $100,000,000. Inasmuch as they have been paid for constructing this line, why should they claim in perpetuity that they should receive more because their grade is 2-2? If they have been paid, why should there not be an equalization and why should they not give us in British Columbia the same benefit as they extend to other provinces?
I want to deal for a moment with one or two statements made by the Minister of Railways, and I am coming to his argument last. He said that in the United States there is no grade such as the Canadian National has-well, he did not mention the Canadian National. I would point out that in the United States there are heavier grades than the Canadian Pacific has to contend with, because the land in Canada slopes downward to the north pole, Edmonton being
1.800	feet lower than Calgary, and Calgary
1.800	feet lower than Seattle. The further south you go the higher the grade.

speechtext:
I am sorry I misunderstood the minister; I thought he was speaking of grades on railways. To speak for a moment on rates, it is true that in the United States they have only one rate, but I doubt very much the minister's statement that it is equal to or comparable with our domestic rate. I have not the time to go into that, but I put the figures on record last session for the information of the then Minister of Railway, Mr. Manion, and I have them under my hand. I would point out to the minister that while they have only one rate from the wheat fields to the state of Washington, they carry all grain, bran, flour, shorts, or wheat at that rate, and it is lower, whereas in Canada, on grain going west, there is a temporary rate that applies only to feed grain, but on fifty per cent of the requirements of the poultry men and dairy men we are still called upon to pay 41J cents.
The minister has appealed to me to withdraw the bill for the time being. This is a matter that is giving me a great deal of concern at the moment. I am not unmindful
that, after all what I am after is results, not for myself but for the people of British Columbia; and as I pointed out, I intend to keep fighting this cause, 'because we have justice on our side. Not always does a person get results because he has justice on his side, but I believe we have a case that cannot be successfully refuted; certainly it has not been so far.
I am also not unmindful that in 1931, when I came to my first session of parliament, the position was almost the same. There was an appeal then before the governor in council, and I, coming into the house for the first time, placed a resolution on the order paper. The then prime minister, now leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) rose and stated, truly, I think, that his government had not yet had time to hear that appeal, and he asked me at that time if I would withdraw the resolution, promising, so he stated, that just as soon as parliament was prorogued they would give the matter attention. I, being in those days younger and more innocent, agreed to this. When I came back the following year the situation was exactly the same; nothing had been done. I was wondering, when the new minister of railways was making the same suggestion, whether I was going to be caught a second time, because "once bitten, twice shy." However, as the appeal to the governor in council at this time on behalf of the province has been lodged by myself I am inclined to do this, but I warn the minister and the government now that I am looking for some practical results, and I shall not 'be content if the suggestion by the minister is being made merely by way of a sop. This is the beginning of a new parliament. I expect far more results from it than I did from the last, because, as I stated, Mr. Speaker, invariably the party to your left have taken the stand that the matter is one for the board of railway commissioners, and I have pointed out that an appeal to that board is absolutely useless if we are to expect any results. So I have come to the highest court in the land, the court of the common people, to plead on behalf of British Columbia, and if I withdraw the bill for the time being it is with a view to getting action from the present government, and with the warning, not a threat, that if something further is not done they will certainly have a battle on their hands.

maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext:
What policy has the government regarding memorials on battlefields in Ontario? Large amounts haive been voted for memorials around the city of Quebec. I do not object to that because they are valuable, but if one province has been overlooked since confederation it is Ontario and its historic places. Take the Niagara district, rich in history. Little or nothing has been done except for the erection of a few cairns here and there. Starting at the Niagara river at lake Ontario, what have you? Old Fort Mississauga, a heap of ruins. Near the steamboat landing is old Fort George, and the place where the first parliament of this country met at Newark, now Niagara. Further up the river are Queenston Heights and Lundy's Lane. But this district has been altogether overlooked. We need to take a lesson from the people of the United States in regard to preserving these historic places. Lord Macaulay in his History of England said in regard to memorials of the siege of Londonderry in the north of Ireland, as follows:
The humble tombs of the . . . captains have been carefully sought out, repaired, and embellished. It is impossible not to respect the sentiment which indicates itself by these tokens. It is a sentiment which belongs to the higher and purer part of human nature, and which adds not a little to the strength of states. A people which takes no pride in the noble achievements of remote ancestors will never achieve anything worthy to be remembered. . . .
The battlefields of the war of 1812 are heaps of ruins, while just across the river at Fort Niagara in the state of New York, a

Supply-Miscellaneous-Battlefields
district visited by millions of people, we see what the United States government have done to the old fort on that side. Ontario is entitled to better treatment in this matter. I have every confidence in the new minister, because I know he frequently visits this district and the city from which I come. I raised this question in the house when I first came here in 1922 but there has been no improvement. On the United States side they have spent large sums of money at Fort Niagara and rebuilt the fort, and spent a lot of money on the memorials there.
There is a decrease of $1,839 in this vote.
I venture to say that hardly a five cent piece has been spent in Ontario except for a few little cairns or slabs at about $1.75 a yard with a little inscription on them. That is not fair. In that same Niagara district there is Ridgeway where battles were fought in 1866, and in 1867 the Fenian raid. In the city I come from we celebrated last year the one hundredth anniversary of the incorporation of the city. Its first mayor was the grandfather of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who did much for responsible government in this country and reasserted the principles of magna charts, and the Prime Minister attended that centennial and did honour to the memory of William Lyon Mackenzie. I hope the day will come when there will be adequate memorials in Ontario, marldng the events of the war of 1812, and in the prairie provinces for the Northwest rebellion and other historic events. I do not object to the money that has been spent on the battlefields around Quebec, but other parts of the country should have similar treatment. I hope the new minister will give this his consideration.
We are looking for tourists. When they come to Ontario, many pass through Fort Erie where an important battle was fought, and they see on the battleground there an ancient building covered with chewing tobacco advertisements. At Chattanooga in the south, in the valley of the Cumberland where Grant made his reputation there are about forty-six monuments on that battlefield about thirty miles long, where each of the states built a monument about the size of our Brock's monument. In the village of Chippawa what have we? I saw something in the newspaper recently about Laura Secord, and the shabby treatment of her portrait. In the village of Chippawa where the power canal has been diverted there is a little bit of a cottage on the south side of the street w'here she lived, but hardly anything showing that is where Laura Secord lived. The old home in the village of Queenston is nowhere,
and at Queenston where William Lyon Mackenzie had a printing newspaper office, and where the first printing press was set up in upper Canada the building is a mass of ruins. You would almost think you were in Belgium during the war.
Last summer was the fiftieth anniversary of the Northwest rebellion. There are only a few left of the old boys who went to the northwest at that time, I think less than a score in Toronto of the Queen's Own, the Grenadiers and the Governor General's Bodyguard commanded by the late Colonel Denison. These men went out to the northwest in 1885 to prevent this country from being dislocated and dismembered, and to avenge the death of that great patriot, Thomas Scott. There was a meeting last summer in Winnipeg, but they could not get sufficient public support to send about two hundred men from Halifax, Montreal and Toronto to visit the old places. The battlefields of Cut Knife, Batoche and others should be marked out and preserved. These battlefields in our own country should be marked as well as the battlefields overseas. We are behind the times. We had many millions to spend on railways but apparently almost nothing for this purpose. I commend the work which the department has been doing; they have certainly done good work, but there should be equality of treatment for all the provinces.
I believe in a principle for confederation in the words of the old Cornish battle cry: Each for all and all for each. That should be the confederation battle cry for this parliament. Parliament is supposed to be a club where a member can express his views, whatever they may be. In my opinion the rising generation should be given a practical demonstration of the sentiment of preserving these historic places of interest throughout our country, I suggest that something of a practical nature should be done to commemorate Laura Secord, and that something should be done to restore the home where she lived in the village of Chippawa and at Queenston, and that section of the Niagara district, and to restore the ruins of the various historic places of the war of 1812-1814. We should have something to commemorate those people who did so much in the early days towards building up our country. I hope the minister, who has been in our section quite a number of times and has always been welcomed there, will see that something is done in the Niagara district in connection with this matter.
I commend the good work done by the battlefields commission at Quebec. The late Colonel Denison of Toronto was one of the first commissioners and was appointed by the Laurier government. In my opinion the work

Supply-Miscellaneous-Battlefields
which was done in Quebec should be extended to all the other provinces of confederation, where there are historic places connected with the early history of this country.

speechtext: I freely confess that this work, which is of a highly scientific nature, is a little beyond the range of my knowledge or experience. 1 may say however that the work has to do with measurements as to the positions of stars, and the relation of those measurements to measurement of time. Communications by radio are maintained with other observatories, and as a result we are able to have very accurate time. For instance, in Ottawa we have six hundred electrical clocks, three of which are in this chamber. It is important to have the correct time, otherwise the [DOT]hon. member for Winnipeg North might lose some time in one of the speeches he makes to the house. Then, the observatory studies sun spots and their effect on climatic conditions and plant life. Recent theories of the physicists indicate that sun spots have a material bearing on mundane matters, and we in Canada wish to make our contribution to the study of these problems. Then, the seismographical branch does an important work; when earthquakes take place we are able to do our share towards ascertaining where they may be. Then, there is the abstruse problem of getting an accurate method of measuring gravity. What particular relation this has to the ordinary affairs of the country I am unable to say, but I believe it is of considerable importance.

speechtext: It is desirable that the minister should make as complete a statement as he can with respect to this whole Indian problem. I confess that during the last few years I have become considerably interested in it, and if the minister will take it up in detail and give us some idea of the present situation I think that would be appreciated by the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext:
I confess that my knowledge of the whole Indian problem in Canada is not as intimate as I could wish, but I might say in a general way that the Indian population in Canada to-day is about 112,000,
tMr. Spence. 1
and is increasing. The fact that it is increasing makes the Indian problem deserving of the attention of public authorities with a view to studying the best methods for bringing education to the Indians, making them selfsupporting, and generally improving their situation. Undoubtedly a very .large number of Indians are on relief at the moment. I am speaking from memory, but I think I am correct when I say that about one-third of the Indian population of Canada has been on relief for the last two or three years. The rather superficial study that I have been able to give to Indian problems since I took charge of the department has inclined me to the view that the administration is rather expensive; that it costs a considerable amount of money and probably might be improved in some respects. I hope to study this problem before I come again to submit estimates to the committee, if it is my good fortune to do so.
There are further problems in connection with education. In this connection we sometimes run into a rather delicate situation. It is sometimes found that two or three denominations are carrying on their good work in one community, and this ocaesionally creates a problem. There is as well the question of hospitalization. If we are to discharge our obligations to the Indians in this connection, this matter will stand a very considerable amount of study. There is the problem of bringing the Indians to a better understanding of the methods of the white man and his way of living. At times I do not think we have acted wisely in this respect. In western Canada and in some parts of Ontario there are Indians who are making substantial progress towards becoming self-supporting. This is being achieved mainly through agriculture, but in the more remote parts of the country trapping and fishing, the traditional occupations of the Indian, are practically his only means of support. Our Indians are scatterred from Halifax to Vancouver and from the international boundary to the Arctic circle and one realizes the magnitude of the problem when this vast area is considered. I do not know that there is much more that I can actd to this statement.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was very glad to hear the minister say that he is going to look carefully into the whole question of the administration of the Department of Indian Affairs. I notice also that in every case there is a considerable amount of supplies. Upon looking over these items I can see a good deal in the old saying: Lo, the poor Indian. speechtext:
The fact that the Indian population is increasing is in itself prima facie evidence that the Indians are being well looked after. Prior to a few years ago the Indian agents were not always medical men, nor are they yet; but an effort was made during the last regime to provide that if possible they should have some medical training. The result is, I believe, that this is the first time a report has been made to the house of an increase in the Indian population. My memory is that it was shrinking a few years ago; but during the last few years an effort has been made, whenever vacancies have occurred, to appoint as Indian agent, if possible, a medical man. As a result the children have been better cared for; tuberculosis has been brought under control; disease has diminished, and the habits of life of the Indians have improved.
I cannot speak of the Indians in the maritime provinces. The report I received with respect to them on one occasion was rather alarming, and a special effort was made to have some specific relief afforded them. They were in a rather bad way. In Quebec, apart from the large bands, there are small bands scattered over many sections of the province, and in Ontario, apart from the large reserves, there are numbers of bands of Indians. When we get into western Canada we find that usually they have excellent reserves. At Macleod the Bloods have a very fine reserve from which they receive substantial revenues. The Blackfoot Indians have sold large quantities of their land, sometimes by public auction and sometimes not, and considerable sums of
Supply-Indian Affairs

money have gone into their endowment fund. They have been greatly improved in their status during the last few years, for they have been fairly well to do. The Stony Indians, west of Calgary, are in a bad way. They are hunters and fishermen and during the last few years have suffered acutely. A good deal of money has been expended in improving facilities at Morley, and perhaps they are better off than they were a while ago. So far as British Columbia is concerned, reports from that province indicate that many of the Indians are in a pretty bad way, and a special effort was made to look after many of them.
I have been astounded at the enormous sums of money we have had to spend to accomplish the results. The year before last the situation was very acute, and when you realize that $4,000,000 has been spent on about
112,000	Indians, who themselves possess adequate resources in the way of reserves, I can only say that the closest supervision ought to be exercised over administration. I believe in many cases they get rations, and they have treaty money distributed to them under the terms of surrender they made to their interests in lands and the taking up of reserves. They have a certain sum in the way of treaty money, and then they have the interest on their own funds. I understand that they utilize their own funds for the construction of buildings.
One of the most difficult problems is that connected with education; I believe it is the outstanding problem in that regard. My memory is that the cost per head in connection with these institutions is what absorbs a very substantial part of this appropriation. That is a matter which perhaps can be carefully considered during the recess, but there are grave and delicate difficulties, as the hon. gentleman has said, by reason of the possibility of differences arising with respect to the religious denominations that should look after particular bands of Indians.
In the far north, most distressing tales came down two years ago of the condition of the Indians, and I hope that during this very hard winter they have not experienced the hardship they did that year; for in the western provinces, where the cold has been intense, the condition of the Indians in the last few weeks has been very trying. I think the relief measures afforded them have been as nearly adequate as possible.
Canada, I believe, has discharged its obligations to its wards about as well as has any country in the world, but during the last ten years there has been a decided increase in expenditures. The Indians have

been receiving medical attention and care which they never had before, and with the rations they have received they have been in a much better position, very much better as a matter of fact, than have many other sections of our population. I realize the minister's difficulty, and it is only fair to say that he is not responsible for expenditures that have occurred during the last fiscal year; he is responsible only for the sums he is asking for and for the work that will be done during the next fiscal year under existing conditions. But what is the S100,000 for?

Mr. WOOD1: I was not expecting that this vote would be considered to-night. I am sorry I have not before me the information I should have liked to present concerning the Six Nations Indians who happen to reside in	the	constituency I	have	the honour	to
represent. Of the 112,000 Indians in Canada
5,000	live in the reserve adjacent to the city of	Brantford, and in	the	constituency	ofBrant.	In my view	they	should not	beclassed with the average Indian of the dominion, when we learn that about thirty-three per cent of the Indians are on relief. From a conversation I had recently with the superintendent at Brantford I learned that of	the	5,000 Indians	in the Six Nations
reserve only eighty-one are on relief. That would seem to indicate that they are capable in the discharge of their duties and are able to take care of themselves. For those reasons they have advanced more than many others of the aborigines of the dominion.
I believe that until about three years ago they administered their own educational system, but for some reason or another that privilege was taken away from them. I have not been able to ascertain the reason. The department gave the excuse that they had appropriated the whole of the education of Indians on reserves, and that because of that they must take away from the Indians the administration of their schools. In passing may I observe that the Indians built their own schools from their own band funds, and prior to that time had contributed about half of the cost of their own education. They enjoy a reasonable amount of autonomy due to the fact that they elect their own council, and it seems to me it was most unfortunate that the Indians were deprived of a degree of autonomy which, by virtue of their advance, we had the right to encourage them to go further; we ought to give them more autonomy and more control over their affairs, in so far as they are able to manage them.
Supply-Indian Affairs

In that way we shall make good citizens of them.
In the few moments I shall speak-and I shall not take too long-may I state that the Indians on the Six Nations reserve are in a somewhat different position from that of the average of the aborigines of Canada, because they compare very favourably with our United Empire Loyalists. An agreement was made between Captain Joseph brant and the British government whereby he w'ould extend his loyalty towards the British at the time of the American revolution. The loyalists were granted certain concessions if they would remain true to the British crown. They came to Canada and were granted a piece of land extending six miles on either side of the Grand river, from its mouth to its source. They did not need all that land and for that reason they sold a portion of it. The money was set aside and was held in trust in Canada as a trust fund for the maintenance of the Indians. This was a good business proposition, and I believe we have every reason to commend the Indians for their astuteness in having a bank account. I only wish the government had as good a bank account as have those Indians, because if that were so we would be in a much better position than we are in to-day. The matter upon which I am speaking has been a perennial subject. I believe my predecessor, Mr. Smoke, described conditions possibly better than I am in a position to do, because I know he has made a study of the subject. At the present time I am going through eighty-six pages of legal phraseology. So far I have gone only about half way through, but it has been my endeavour to learn the history oi the Six Nations Indians.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext: Read Mr. Smoke's speech and you will get the story.

maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext:
Yes, and I commend Mr. Smoke for his approach to the subject. Unfortunately I have not been able to get all the facts in the short time I have had at my disposal, but to the best of my ability I have endeavoured to do so in my own way. For that reason I shall not go into detail, because I do not wish to misplace the ancient characters, or to put them in a wrong light.
It seems, however, that about one hundred years ago a scheme knowm as the Grand river navigation project was devised. It was incorporated in 1832. Trustees were empowered to enter upon the crown lands, or the lands belonging to the Six Nations Indians, after making compensation. The funds belonging to these Indians were at that time held by trustees. In 1832 the Hon. J. H. Dunn, then

Receiver General of Upper Canada, had charge of the public moneys of the then province. He was an active exponent of the policy of canal construction, and held the office of president of the Welland Canal Company. The Grand River Navigation Company acted more or less as a subsidiary and was to supply the water to the Welland canal. By virtue of that arrangement the two companies worked together.
Mr. Dunn filled the further position of trustee of the Six Nations Indians. He appears to have taken a most active part in their money affairs. On April 3, 1834, an order in council was passed stating the Indians desired that their moneys invested in British funds should be transferred to Canada to be invested in provincial debentures or other government securities. I shall not go into details as to the ramifications of the charters or supplementary letters patent, in view of the various changes in the financial structure, but briefly I would state that they did get a promise from Sir John Colborne, the then Lieutenant Governor of Upper Canada, to assist them in an endeavour to form a company to permit trade in western Ontario via the Grand river. He was successful in getting sufficient interest among men who had money to invest to organize the company.
As time went on the Buffalo and Goderich line was built, which was another change that took place in the transportation system, thus impairing the possibilities of the Grand River Navigation Company. The competition of the railway would largely impair the possibilities of the canal. These men found that they were going to be left in a precarious position. For some reason, of which at the present time I am not aware, they wished to withdraw their obligations and pledge to Sir John Colborne and, to make a long story short, those who were responsible substituted the Indian funds to purchase stock, and put those funds into a precarious investment.
The association of the Receiver General with the Grand River Navigation Company placed the government in a rather unfortunate position, for it meant that they were investing funds which they held in trust for the Indians in a company in which some of them were personally interested. You will see, Mr. Chairman, that the security of the funds of the Six Nations Indians was thus jeopardized, and the Indians in consequence feel that they have been more or less exploited through this scheme of organizing a joint stock company and investing it in their funds which were held in trust for them by the government of the day. Whether the powers of a trust company had been defined at that time or not, it is

Supply-Indian Affairs
not lawful, as I understand the matter, for a trustee to invest in a joint stock company funds committed to his care.
It might be said that all this happened one hundred years ago and that we have no obligation to-day. While there may not be a legal obligation-and I cannot speak as to that-undoubtedly there is a moral obligation, and that moral obligation was incurred through the filching from the coffers of the Indians of this $160,000 of trust funds which belonged to the Six Nations. I do not say that this was done with dishonest intent; it might have been done with the intention of serving a good purpose, but the unfortunate point is that the money was held in trust for the Indians and the government had no right to invest it in a joint stock company.

I am afraid that the claim of the Six Nations Indians, a claim that originated over a hundred years ago, to $160,000, with accumulated interest, is one that the government could not entertain. I do not know the merits or demerits of the claim that the hon. member for Brant has put forward. Since this question originated 102 years ago or thereabouts, the federal government as we know it to-day cannot be responsible for the matter. If my memory of history is correct, this happened during the time when Upper Canada was still being governed as a crown colony. The hon. member spoke to me some little time ago about this question, but I have not had an opportunity of going into it. I am afraid I cannot hold out any hope that we will meet a claim, which originated over 100 years ago for $160,000 with interest to date. I am afraid that a serious consideration of such a proposal would send my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) to the hospital.
There are some 6,000 Indians in the reserve to which my hon. friend refers. From information I have been able to obtain, I understand they have done remarkably well. There is a question whether the Indian Act, which after all is the act under which matters pertaining to the Indian population of Canada are administered, comes into conflict with the suggestion he makes. At the moment I cannot pass any critical judgment on his request. My information is that the majority of the teachers in the schools on the Brant reserve are of Indian origin. My hon. friend shakes his head. Perhaps my information is incorrect, but I understand that at any rate a number of the teachers have been trained from Indians who have been pupils in the years immediately past. It is desirable as a general rule that the Indians should be made as independent as possible of outside assistance. No one would have greater pleasure than I if the Indians throughout Canada could attain a position whereby they would be not only self-supporting but able to look after such matters as education and other things as their white brothers do.

speechtext: I listened with considerable interest to what the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood) had to say about the funds which were invested in the Grand River Navigation Company. Prior to the change which took place in 1932, as described by the hon. gentleman, there was considerable jealousy and quarrelling among the Indians as to who should teach in their schools. No; I was disfranchised by the previous administration and forced to move eastward. Nevertheless I take an interest in Caughnawaga and I notice that the leader of the opposition has still a weakness for it. I daresay he recalls his last visit there. In that reserve, which is one of the largest in Quebec, the Indians have a territory of approximately
11,000	acres of good farm land which is practically without cultivation except by ' white people who rent the farms. Very often we have requests from these white people, who are on the reserve with the permission of the Department of Indian Affairs, to investigate complaints they make to the effect that they are not being well treated. In some instances these white men are barely tolerated on the reserve, and not being able to get work they are on relief. They have not the means of supporting themselves and they are in a peculiar position. Though they live on the reserve, the Department of Indian Affairs is not obliged to make provision for them, and the provincial government, under the relief laws, is not bound to support them. They are therefore left without support.
It is a matter of importance for the department to come to the rescue of these white men in view of the fact that the department itself allows them to live there. A considerable quantity of land there has been abandoned, and I suggest to the government that it would be wise to look into the situation and see whether it would not be better to allow these Indians to sell this very important piece of land, either by auction or otherwise. It is important inasmuch as it is near so large a centre as Montreal, and the Indians are not inclined to cultivate it. They are rather inclined to specialize in hazardous work, such as employment in connection with the Dominion Bridge Company or other steel works. This is their only occupation, and if the Department of Indian Affairs were allowed to sell this large area the amount derived from its
sale could be used for the benefit of the Indians themselves and would assist the department in the administration of the reserve.
I make this suggestion to the department in good faith, hoping that they will take action. As the hon. member for Brant stated-, the Indians of Caughnawaga generally speaking are likely to attain the same level as the so-called civilized white man, and I think if they were given more freedom, if they could inspire the government with a little more confidence and were allowed to sell their land on certain conditions, within a few years this large area of good land could be disposed of, one farm after another, so that the people in the surrounding district might use it for farming purposes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext: How many Indians are there?

maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext:
Around 3,800.
Mr.CRERAR: Less than that; a little under 3,000.

maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext:
As matters stand now, it would cost the Department of Indians Affairs a considerable sum to take care of these Indians properly from the point of view of education and hygiene. For the most part the village is built on rook, so that the construction of sewers and a water system would cost a great deal; the department would have to spend too much. For this reason, indicated by the officials of the department when I investigated the matter, the inhabitants are unaible to follow the rules of hygiene, and the doctors themselves say that in Caughnawaga some of the diseases that are prevalent on the reserve are undermining the health of the population. I believe the population of this particular reserve is diminishing, owing to the fact that at present the department is unable to give the Indians the legitimate attention they should receive.
If the government would accept this sug-' gestion and allow the Indians to sell their farms, retaining the proceeds at their disposal, the majority of the Indians would follow the ordinary pursuits of life, while those who preferred to retain their status could be more easily taken care of.
Another aspect of the question which interests me is hospitalization. If it is as it was when I was member for Laprairie-Napier-ville, they have an old building as their hospital which is far too small for the needs of the reserve. If the department were to spend the amount required for that purpose the cost would be considerable, because I think it would have to erect a new building. I
Supply-Indian Affairs

do not want to embarrass the minister. I make this suggestion only with the hope that the department will study the necessity of applying this policy. But may I know from the minister how much money has been voted this year for Caughnawaga, and especially how much is going to be applied for the hospital and for education?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext: So far as disposing of a part of the reserve for farming purposes to white men, as the hon. member suggested, is concerned, it is necessary in all cases to get the approval of the band to the surrender of any of their property. I am not entirely familiar with conditions surrounding such a surrender in Quebec, but I understand that the point arises that if a surrender is made it has to be made to the crown.

maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext: I think the provincial government, if the question were stated seriously, could enter into an agreement whereby if the land is to be abandoned by the Department of Indian Affairs it would not revert to the crown as represented by the provincial government, but the Quebec government could come to an agreement allowing the Department of Indian Affairs to sell that land. I know this question involves some difficulties which were not solved in the past, but I discussed this matter with the provincial government some years ago, and if my memory serves me aright, I believe a solution of the problem can be found.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext: The consent of the Indians would be required to any transaction of that kind. With regard to the other point that my hon. friend mentioned, namely, the presence of white people on the reserves, that presents a rather difficult problem. It has occasionally happened that a white man has married an Indian woman of the reserve. He may die, and then the Indian woman, who has taken the status of her husband, may with her children return to the reserve. Under the [DOT]Indian Act they are no longer Indians, but of course they are living on the Indian reserve, and the practice, I am informed, has been to supply them with relief where that is necessary. This is one of the problems that arise perhaps inevitably in the administration of Indian affairs. I shall be very glad to keep in mind the observations made by my hon. friend. I am sorry to say that I am not in a position to state just how far we shall be able to go in meeting his wishes.

maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext:
Referring again to the question of money that was invested by the crown some years ago in the Grand River Navigation Company and which belonged to the Six Nations Indians, I discussed this matter at one time with a former Minister of the

Interior, the Hon. Charles Stewart. He told me at that time that in lieu of this, the government had been granting some ten thousand dollars annually for the upkeep of the roads on this reservation. Is that item of ten thousand dollars included in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext:
I am sorry that at the
moment I cannot give a definite answer to my hon. friend's question. My deputy tells me that some special grants are given to this reserve. Whether or not one is given in consideration of a claim which they believe they have against the crown, and to which the hon. member for Brant has referred, I cannot say.

maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext: I should not like the minister to have the impression that I said "in consideration of this claim"; the amount was rather as a satisfaction to them in lieu of the claim itself. I know this money has been expended, and very well expended, on the reservation for the past few years in the building of roads, although the roads are not nearly completed, and I suggest to the minister that the grant should be continued if possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext:
We shall have that under
consideration.

maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext: Do I understand the minister to say that compulsory education is definitely established on the Indian reserves as well as in other public school systems in Ontario or the dominion? I could not catch his answer because of interruptions. I am referring to compulsory education.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext: According to the information I have, it was intended under the Indian Act that educational facilities should be made available to Indian children as fa.r as possible, and that where they were available the Indian children should take advantage of them. In that sense there is a limit to compulsion. But my hon. friend probably knows that in attempting to enforce compulsory education, even in ordinary white communities, certain difficulties are encountered. In Indian communities those difficulties are not less; perhaps they are increased.

maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext: Is the adolescent age still applicable to Indian children the same as it is in other communities? The adolescent age is sixteen years.

maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext:
May I ask
whether there is any allocation of that nineteen thousand dollars plus for the building and repair of houses in the Cowichan reserve?

Unemployment-Relief Camps

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext:
I cannot say at the
moment. If the Cowichan reserve deserves some of the appropriation it is probably getting it.

maintopic: ANALYSIS OF CONCESSIONS GRANTED TO CANADA BASED ON UNITED STATES IMPORTS FROM CANADA-CALENDAK YEAR, 1929
speechtext: There are two problems I want to bring to the attention of the Indian department. One is connected with the extension of the Timiskaming and Northern Ontario railway from Cochrane to Moosonee. That has created a new situation.
